text: Edmund Gettier's 1963 paper "Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?" runs just three pages in the journal Analysis. Its two counterexamples set off decades of work on what knowledge is.
Russell and Whitehead's Principia Mathematica does not complete its proof that 1 + 1 = 2 until Volume II (1912), where the authors remark: "The above proposition is occasionally useful."

Plutarch recorded the puzzle of Theseus's ship, repaired plank by plank until no original wood was left. Thomas Hobbes added a twist: rebuild the old planks into a second ship, and both can claim to be the original.

In Newcomb's problem, a near-perfect predictor puts $1 million in a box only if it foresees you refusing a second box of $1,000. Nozick reported in 1969 that people find the answer obvious, yet split almost evenly.

Buridan's ass, starving between two equal bales of hay, appears nowhere in Jean Buridan's surviving writings. The puzzle goes back to Aristotle; critics likely pinned it on Buridan to mock his theory of the will.

The classic wording of Occam's razor, "entities must not be multiplied beyond necessity", is not found in William of Ockham's writings. A close version appears in a 1639 commentary by the Irish friar John Punch.

Descartes first published "I think, therefore I am" in French, as "je pense, donc je suis", in his Discourse on the Method (1637). The Latin "cogito, ergo sum" came later, in his Principles of Philosophy (1644).

Just before calling religion "the opium of the people", Marx called it "the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world". The full 1844 passage is more sympathetic than the famous fragment.

In 1938 the Franciscan priest Herman Van Breda found more than 40,000 pages of Edmund Husserl's shorthand manuscripts in Nazi Germany and got them out to Leuven, Belgium, where the Husserl Archives still keep them.
Martin Heidegger's Being and Time (1927) is a fragment. Its introduction lays out a plan of six divisions, but only the first two were ever published, and he abandoned the rest.
Albert Camus died on January 4, 1960, in a car driven by his friend Michel Gallimard. An unused train ticket was found in his pocket; he had planned to travel back to Paris by train.
Jean-Paul Sartre declined the 1964 Nobel Prize in Literature. He said he always declined official honors, because a writer should not allow himself to be turned into an institution.

Jeremy Bentham asked for his body to be preserved and displayed. His skeleton, dressed in his own clothes and topped with a wax head, sits in a glass case at University College London; the real head is stored separately.

The young Wang Yangming, by his own account, sat before bamboo for seven days trying to grasp its principle, as Zhu Xi advised. He found nothing, fell ill, and later taught that principle lies in the mind.
Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly, flitting happily about. On waking he could not tell whether he was Zhuangzi who had dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming it was Zhuangzi.

Classical Indian Nyaya logic set out an argument in five steps. Its stock example: the hill has fire, because it has smoke; wherever there is smoke there is fire, as in a kitchen; so the hill has fire.
Jean-François Lyotard's The Postmodern Condition (1979), the book that made "postmodern" a byword in philosophy, began as a report on knowledge commissioned by the universities council of Quebec.

In 1992 Cambridge dons forced a rare vote over an honorary degree for Jacques Derrida, and 19 scholars, mostly philosophers and including W. V. Quine, wrote to The Times against it. Derrida won, 336 votes to 204.

After seeing Andy Warhol's Brillo Boxes in 1964, Arthur Danto wrote "The Artworld", asking what makes an artwork differ from an identical-looking object. His answer: a context of theory the eye cannot see.
"Never literary attempt was more unfortunate than my Treatise of Human Nature. It fell dead-born from the press." (David Hume, My Own Life, 1776)
"Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent." (Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, 1922)

In 1902, as the second volume of Gottlob Frege's Basic Laws of Arithmetic was in press, a letter from Bertrand Russell showed that one of its axioms led to a contradiction. Frege added an appendix facing the damage.

Frank Jackson's 1982 thought experiment about Mary, a color scientist raised in a black-and-white room, became a classic argument against physicalism. Jackson himself later rejected it and became a physicalist.
In 1787 Kant wrote that logic had not advanced a single step since Aristotle and seemed to be complete. In 1879 Gottlob Frege's Begriffsschrift rebuilt logic from the ground up.

At Antonio Gramsci's 1928 trial, the fascist prosecutor reportedly demanded that his brain be stopped from working for twenty years. In prison Gramsci filled notebooks with nearly 3,000 pages of political thought.

David Chalmers named "the hard problem of consciousness" in a 1994 talk in Tucson: why brain processes are accompanied by felt experience at all. Explaining what the brain does is the easy part; this one remains open.

"Cretans are always liars", a line credited to the Cretan Epimenides, became a stock example of the liar paradox. The New Testament letter to Titus quotes it and solemnly adds that the testimony is true.

Ferdinand de Saussure never wrote the Course in General Linguistics (1916) that launched structuralism. After his death two colleagues compiled it from students' lecture notes, though neither had attended the course.
The trolley problem began in a 1967 paper on abortion by Philippa Foot, who imagined the driver of a runaway tram choosing between tracks. Judith Jarvis Thomson gave the puzzle its name in 1976.

On October 13, 1806, as French troops entered Jena, Hegel wrote that he had seen Napoleon, "this world-soul", riding out to reconnoiter. He had just mailed off parts of his manuscript of the Phenomenology of Spirit.
